era.title: The gate behind the wire, 1987
era.summary: In 1987 the Brandenburg Gate stood inside the closed border strip, its Pariser Platz an empty, floodlit security zone, and the exact spot of this stop was not a normal public viewpoint. A reinforced anti-tank wall three metres thick ran directly in front of the gate, and a wing of the building housed an information centre that GDR citizens were not allowed to visit. That June, West Berlin's "Concert for Berlin" drew ever larger crowds on the East side towards the gate, and clashes with police along Unter den Linden were described as the most serious outbreak of public discontent in East Berlin in nearly ten years. Ronald Reagan spoke at the gate on 12 June 1987; details of surfaces, lighting and individual prices in 1987 are thin in the sources consulted.
funFacts: A wing of the gate housed an information centre for visiting delegations, mostly foreign; most East Germans did not know it existed.
The Wall directly in front of the gate was reinforced into an anti-tank barrier three metres thick.
On 12 June 1987 Ronald Reagan said at the gate: "Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!"
From the building of the Wall onward nothing was done to maintain the Quadriga; restorers later found extensive rust in its internal steelwork.
A single inner-city fare on East Berlin public transport was 20 pfennig, and a journey within East Berlin cost 30 pfennig.

sceneBrief.description: Exactly the framing of the photograph: standing on Pariser Platz on the East Berlin side at eye level, looking west straight at the Brandenburg Gate, the quadriga on top facing the viewer, the same size and position in the frame. In 1987 this is the GDR border zone: the gate is soot-grey and weathered, the square in front of it is closed to the public and almost empty, with a low white-and-red barrier fence across it and a sign forbidding entry. Through the columns the grey concrete Berlin Wall with its rounded top runs across behind the gate, and beyond it a watchtower. Two East German border guards in grey-green uniforms and peaked caps stand by the barrier. A GDR flag on a pole beside the gate. Overcast sky.

sceneBrief.surroundings: Seen from eye height on Pariser Platz in the East Berlin border zone in 1987. Ahead (west), the Brandenburg Gate with the Berlin Wall curving behind it and a concrete watchtower. To the left and right, the square is mostly empty ground where the bombed buildings were cleared, with a few bare plane trees, lamp posts and the plain side walls of East German buildings. Behind the viewer (east), the start of Unter den Linden with its lime trees and grey East German facades, a few Trabants parked, people walking at a distance. Overcast sky.

guide.name: Karin Vogt
guide.role: Tram conductor on the lines running to the eastern end of Unter den Linden
guide.bio: I have worked the trams out of Mitte for eleven years, punching tickets and calling the stops, and I know this end of Unter den Linden better than my own street. These days the cars stop well short of the gate, and my passengers lean over to look at the lights and the fences before we turn back.
guide.appearance: Woman of about forty, sturdy and practical, short permed brown hair, wearing a dark blue GDR transport uniform jacket with a small badge, a grey skirt, thick tights and sensible flat shoes, a ticket punch hanging on a strap.
guide.script: I'm Karin Vogt, and I run the tickets on the tram down Unter den Linden. Put in your twenty pfennig, thirty if you stay inside the city, but mind the machines — the coins and the tickets don't always agree. We stop short of the gate now; the last stretch is closed, fences and a barrier across the road. You can stand and look west: the floodlights, the empty square, the old gate behind the flowerpots and that thick wall. People lean out to see it. The trams are dirty and crowded and they sulk at the first snow, but they get us there. Mind yourself at the crossing. Goodbye!
guide.greeting: You look lost at the barrier — everyone does here. I'm Karin, I run the tickets on the tram; come and stand where the trams turn back and I'll tell you what you're looking at.
